issues.legal_issue: Comparable sales provide a proper method for determining the market value of acquired land when the parties produce evidence of sufficiently similar sales.
material_facts: The compensation appeal concerned a large tract of acquired land, and the parties produced evidence of sales of other lands.
One sale concerned a portion of the acquired land, and another concerned land in its close vicinity; the court accepted these as comparable evidence.
Other sales concerned land in a populous area farther from the acquired land or small plots, and the court found them insufficiently comparable to the large acquired tract.
issues.conclusion: The comparable sales method was appropriate, and the accepted sales provided a proper basis for determining the acquired land’s market value.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 8(3) of the Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952, compensation is intended to approximate the land’s just equivalent value on the acquisition date. The method of valuation depends on the evidence produced. Where evidence of sales of the acquired land or land in its vicinity is available, comparable sales are a healthy criterion: Atmaram v. Collector of Nagpur and Union of India v. Kamlabhai Harjiwandas Parekh. Sales must concern land sufficiently comparable in essential features, and sales of small plots ordinarily should not determine the value of a large tract: Collector of Lakhimpur v. Bhuban Chandra Dutta and Prithvi Raj Taneja v. State of M.P. A sale of part of the acquired land can be a useful criterion: Bangaru Narasingha Rao Naidu v. R.D.O. Vizianagaram.

predicates.land_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.comparable_sale_evidence_present: The parties have produced evidence of sales of the acquired land or land in its vicinity.
predicates.sale_land_similar_in_essential_features: The land covered by the sale evidence is similar to the acquired land in material features such as location and extent.

issues.definition: When a land-compensation appeal includes evidence of sales of land similar in essential features to the acquired land, the comparable sales method is appropriate.

issues.legal_issue: A claim of building potentiality need not independently affect valuation when comparable sales of land form the basis of valuation.
material_facts: The acquired land was valued using sales regarded as comparable to it in essential features.
The owner argued that the acquired land had building potentiality at the time of acquisition.
issues.conclusion: The building-potentiality contention did not require separate consideration because the comparable sales method was being used.
issues.legal_principle: Section 8(3) of the Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952 requires compensation approximating the land’s just equivalent value. Where the comparable sales method is used because the acquired land is comparable in essential features to land covered by sale evidence, building potentiality does not independently determine the valuation in that case. The comparable sales method is recognized as a healthy criterion in Atmaram v. Collector of Nagpur and Union of India v. Kamlabhai Harjiwandas Parekh.

predicates.land_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.comparable_sales_method_used: The court bases the valuation on prices paid in sales of other land.
predicates.acquired_land_compared_on_essential_feat: The acquired land is treated as comparable in essential features to the land covered by the sales.

issues.definition: If comparable sales are used in a land-compensation appeal because the acquired land is similar in essential features to the sold land, building potentiality need not independently control the valuation.

issues.legal_issue: A market valuation that omits a demonstrated local trend of rising land prices should account for that trend.
material_facts: The High Court valued the acquired land by reference to comparable sales but did not account for the trend in local land prices.
Evidence showed increasing prices in the area, including prices for developed plots and a prior compensation award for land purchased at an earlier price.
The Supreme Court added an increment to the High Court’s valuation to reflect the supported price rise.
issues.conclusion: The acquired land’s valuation had to be increased to account for the demonstrated local price rise.
issues.legal_principle: Section 8(3) of the Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952 requires compensation approximating the land’s just equivalent value on the acquisition date. Comparable sale prices may need adjustment for relevant factors not common to the sold land and the acquired land; a supported trend of local price rise is such a factor. The governing just-equivalent principle is stated in Union of India v. Kamlabhai Harjiwandas Parekh.

predicates.land_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land.
predicates.local_price_rise_evidence_present: Evidence in the case indicates that land prices in the relevant area rose over time.
predicates.initial_valuation_omits_supported_price_: The valuation being reviewed does not account for a price rise supported by the evidence.

issues.definition: When evidence in a land-compensation appeal supports a local price rise that the initial valuation omitted, the acquired land’s valuation must account for that rise.

issues.legal_issue: The value of an acquired building should rest on supported valuation evidence and include proven building items omitted from the estimate used.
material_facts: The owner relied on a private engineer’s estimate, but the engineer did not testify and could not be cross-examined; the arbitrator’s inspection report was signed after the award.
A valuation prepared by government public works engineers, scrutinized and approved by senior engineers, was produced through a witness for the owner.
The estimate omitted retaining walls, wire fencing, and a main gate wall, whose value was established in the case.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was justified in relying on the supported public works estimate, but the value of the omitted building items had to be added.
issues.legal_principle: Section 8(3) of the Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952 requires compensation approximating the acquired property’s just equivalent value. A valuation estimate whose maker is not available for examination and whose reliability cannot be tested may be rejected, while a supported estimate can be relied on; proven components omitted from that estimate must also be included to reach the just equivalent price.

predicates.building_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for an acquired building.
predicates.private_estimate_not_tested: The maker of a private valuation estimate did not testify in a way that allowed the estimate to be tested by cross-examination.
predicates.supported_building_estimate_present: A building estimate was supported by relevant professional scrutiny and evidence from a witness.
predicates.omitted_items_proven: The evidence established the value of building components left out of the estimate.

issues.definition: In a building-compensation appeal, a supported estimate is used and proven omitted components are included when the private estimate was not tested.

issues.legal_issue: Solatium for property acquired under the general requisition-and-acquisition framework cannot exceed the benefit available for comparable acquisitions under the applicable State law.
material_facts: The acquired property was in a State whose land acquisition law provided the applicable rate of solatium for acquisitions there.
The owner sought the higher rate available under the Central Land Acquisition Act.
The High Court applied the State-law rate, and the Supreme Court upheld that treatment.
issues.conclusion: The solatium was properly fixed at the rate available under the applicable State law, rather than the higher Central rate.
issues.legal_principle: Section 23(2) of the Rajasthan Land Acquisition Act governed the solatium rate for the property in the State. The court held that acquisition under the Requisitioning and Acquisition of Immovable Property Act, 1952 did not confer a solatium benefit unavailable for land acquired under the State Act.

predicates.acquisition_compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for acquired property.
predicates.property_acquired_under_general_requisit: The property was acquired under a framework for requisitioning and acquiring property rather than directly under the local land acquisition law.
predicates.state_law_sets_solarium_benefit_for_loca: The applicable State law sets the solatium benefit for comparable local acquisitions.

issues.definition: When property is acquired under the general requisition-and-acquisition framework and State law sets the solatium benefit for local acquisitions, the solatium cannot exceed that State-law benefit.
